That difference is structural, not a matter of care: a typed reference is a photograph of the numbering at the moment of writing, and this document has renumbered 3 times. Month-counting instead of day-counting rarely happens once in a document; it is a habit, and habits repeat. (The reverse error also exists — durations counted in days across February in a leap year — so check February-crossing spans with particular care.)

This is one role wearing three titles, almost certainly one per contributing author.

Why it is not a pedantic problem: the manual's training and authorisation clauses will use one of these titles, and a reader holding a different job title on their contract can honestly conclude the clause is not about them. 'Operatives working at height' and 'technicians are trained to level 3' either bind the same people or they don't — the document currently cannot say.

Repair: pick the title that matches the employment contracts (that is the only authority that counts — not the most frequent, not the most senior-sounding), conform every mention, and record the two rejected titles in the style sheet as search terms for future audits. If the business genuinely has three grades, the fix is the opposite: keep the titles and add the one paragraph that distinguishes their duties and authorisations. What the manual cannot do is stay ambiguous.
Our annual report calls the people who pay us three different things. Excerpts in people.txt. Is that a problem, or are the words doing different jobs?
I'll census the three terms and read each use for the job it's doing.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
ANNUAL REPORT EXCERPTS (services firm)
"...our clients value continuity..."
"...customer satisfaction rose..."
"...each user account is assigned..."
"...clients renewing at 91%..."
"...the customer is entitled to a refund..."
"...users may export their data..."
"...new customers joined..."

Census: 'client(s)' 2×, 'customer(s)' 3×, 'user(s)' 2×. Read closely, the words are *almost* doing different jobs — and the 'almost' is the finding.

The defensible pattern underneath: 'clients' for the commercial relationship (continuity, renewals at 91%), 'users' for people operating the product (accounts, data export). That distinction is real and worth keeping — a client firm may have hundreds of users, and renewal statistics and account statistics count different populations.

The problem is 'customer': it appears twice, once for satisfaction and once for a refund entitlement, and in both sentences it means the client. It is the generic word an author reaches for when not thinking, and it blurs the one distinction the report relies on. The refund sentence is the risky one: entitlements should attach to the precisely defined party.

Rule to adopt and record: **client** = the contracting party; **user** = an individual operating the service under a client's account; **customer** = banned in this document set. Apply it as a census-driven edit — every 'customer' occurrence gets read and reassigned deliberately (both here become 'client'), and the final census should show two terms with a stated distinction, not three terms with a vibe.
Our report suite writes dates every way imaginable. The format census is in dates.txt. Assess the damage and give me a ruling.
Reading the census — the mixed slashes are what worry me most, so I'll start there.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
DOCUMENT SET - DATE FORMATS FOUND
Report A: 2027-03-14 (ISO) ×6, 14 March 2027 ×2
Report B: 03/14/2027 ×5, March 14, 2027 ×3
Report C: 14/03/2027 ×4, 2027-03-14 ×1
Appendix: 3/4/2027 ×2

The census shows five formats across four documents, but the real damage is concentrated in one pattern: the all-numeric slash dates. Report B writes 03/14/2027 (US month-first), Report C writes 14/03/2027 (day-first), and the appendix writes 3/4/2027 — which a US reader parses as 4 March and a European reader as 3 April, and *both are plausible dates in context*, so nobody notices the disagreement. Any date where the day is 12 or under is silently ambiguous between the two conventions; only a day above 12 (like the 14s here) reveals which convention a document is using.

Ruling: the suite adopts ISO 8601 (2027-03-14) for all numeric dates — it is unambiguous in every locale, sorts correctly as text, and Report A already uses it most. Long-form dates ('14 March 2027') are acceptable in prose and are also unambiguous; the ban is on all-numeric slash dates in any order.

Conversion warning, and it matters: do not convert Report C's slash dates by pattern-matching alone. 14/03/2027 is provably day-first, but a date like 05/03/2027 inside the same report could have been typed by either habit. Convert the provable ones mechanically; the ambiguous residue — every slash date with both numbers ≤ 12 — goes back to the source data for confirmation. A format cleanup that guesses dates is worse than the mess it fixes.
The product team insists the product is called 'Portal', capital P. The writers use it every which way. The census is in caps.txt. What's the state and the rule?
Reading the census against the registered name.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
DOC SET CENSUS - THE PRODUCT'S NAME
'Portal' (capitalised, as a proper name): 23 occurrences
'portal' (lowercase, generic): 31 occurrences
'PORTAL' (all caps): 4 occurrences, all in headings
Product's registered name: 'Portal'

Of 58 occurrences, the registered form 'Portal' accounts for only 23. Lowercase 'portal' leads with 31 — and some of those 31 are innocent: 'portal' is also an ordinary English word, and a sentence like 'the portal times out' is arguably generic. The all-caps PORTAL (4) is confined to headings and is a styling choice, not an error.

The rule that resolves it without a fight: the product's name is a proper noun — 'Portal' — whenever the specific product is meant, including in sentences where it does something ('Portal times out after 30 minutes'). Lowercase is reserved for the generic concept, which in this document set barely exists — there is one portal product and no discussion of portals in general. So in practice: nearly all 31 lowercase instances should be capitalised, and any genuinely generic use should be rewritten to a different word ('gateway', 'site') so the distinction stays visible.

Apply it by census, not by find-and-replace: a blind replace would also capitalise the word inside quoted customer language and inside the one competitor comparison where 'portal' is generic. Work the 31 occurrences as a list, fix each in context, and re-census to zero unexplained lowercase. Record the rule in the style sheet with the registered name as the authority — writers follow the sheet, not each other's habits.
The annual report was written by two of us and I think we spell differently. The census is in spelling.txt. Diagnose and rule.
Reading the census by author to see whether the split is systematic.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
SPELLING CENSUS - assembled annual report, by section author
Author 1 sections: organise ×4, organisation ×3, behaviour ×2, licence (noun) ×1
Author 2 sections: organize ×5, organization ×2, behavior ×3, license (noun) ×2
Mixed within one section: 0

The split is perfectly systematic — which makes it easy to fix and easy to keep fixed. Author 1 writes British forms throughout (organise, organisation, behaviour, licence as a noun); Author 2 writes American forms throughout (organize, organization, behavior, license). Neither author is internally inconsistent — the census shows zero mixing within a section — so the document's inconsistency is purely a seam problem: the reader crosses it at every section boundary.

The ruling is not mine to make on taste; it follows the audience. The report goes to the group's UK board and UK clients, so the document standardises on British forms: Author 2's sections get the conversion pass (10 variant words by the census, each checked in context — 'license' as a noun becomes 'licence', while any verb use of 'license' stays, since British spelling keeps the verb with an s... precisely: verb 'license', noun 'licence').

Two process points. First, conversion by census list, not global replace — the noun/verb licence distinction is exactly the kind a blind replace destroys. Second, put the variant list into the style sheet as a pre-submission check each author runs on their own sections; a two-author document will drift again the moment a third author joins unless the check lives with the authors rather than with the final editor.

Our framework agreement defines 'Working Day' carefully in clause 1. The operations appendix uses the same term and a supplier claims it means something different there. The definition is in def.txt and the appendix usage is in app-use.txt. Compare them.
I'll set the clause 1 definition against the appendix's usage, element by element.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CLAUSE 1 (definition)
"Working Day" means a day other than a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday in England on which banks in London are open for business.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
APPENDIX 3 (operations) EXCERPTS
"...response within two Working Days of receipt..."
"...the supplier's Working Days are Monday to Saturday, excluding UAE public holidays..."
"...escalation on the next Working Day..."

The supplier is right about the text and the consequences run against the drafter. Clause 1 defines 'Working Day' precisely: not a weekend day, not an English public holiday, London banks open. Appendix 3 then states, in plain words, that 'the supplier's Working Days are Monday to Saturday, excluding UAE public holidays' — a different set of days (Saturdays in, English holidays out, UAE holidays in). The appendix does not misuse the term casually; it affirmatively redefines it, using the capitalised defined form.

So the document contains two definitions of one term, and the response-time obligation ('two Working Days') computes differently under each — by up to several days across a holiday period. In a dispute, a defined term that the document itself uses in two senses is usually construed against the party that drafted it, and in any case cannot be resolved by pointing at clause 1 alone.

Repair, and it is a drafting decision for legal, not an edit I make unilaterally: either (a) the appendix's calendar is the operationally real one — then rename it ('Supplier Working Day', separately defined) and state which term governs the response clock; or (b) clause 1 governs — then the appendix sentence must be deleted and the supplier's Saturday working described without the defined term. Flag it as a blocking item for signature: terminology drift in a definition is not a typo, it is two contracts sharing one document.
The logistics report talks about 'tons' in chapter 3 and chapter 7 and the numbers feel off between them. Chapter 3 is in tons-a.txt, chapter 7 in tons-b.txt. Investigate.
I'll convert both chapters' figures under each possible meaning of 'ton' and see which reading makes them agree.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 3 (excerpt)
"...the terminal handled 12,000 tons in the quarter..." (chapter drafted by the UK team)

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 7 (excerpt)
"...quarterly throughput was 12,000 short tons..." (chapter drafted by the US team)
"...equivalent to 10,886 tonnes..."

The chapters disagree because 'ton' is doing two jobs. Chapter 7 is explicit: 12,000 **short tons** (the US ton of 2,000 lb), and it even gives the conversion — 12,000 short tons × 0.907185 = 10,886 tonnes, matching its printed 10,886. Chapter 3, drafted by the UK team, says '12,000 tons' bare. A UK reader reads that as tonnes or long tons; either way it is not the short ton, and the two chapters' identical numerals describe quantities differing by roughly 9–10%.

So one of the chapters is describing the terminal's quarter wrong: if the true figure is 12,000 short tons (10,886 tonnes), chapter 3 overstates it for its readers; if the true figure is 12,000 tonnes, chapter 7 understates it. The source data — the terminal's own report — is the only arbiter, and the chapters cannot be reconciled until someone checks it.

The standing rule this teaches: in any document that crosses the Atlantic, 'ton' unqualified is a banned word. Write 'tonnes' (metric) as the document standard, with short tons converted and shown in parentheses where the US source data demands it. Add 'ton' to the terminology audit list alongside the other ambiguous units — a unit that changes value by 10% depending on the reader's passport is a consistency defect, not a style choice.
Our metrics glossary defines churn one way; a data analyst says the report body computes it differently. The glossary is in glossary.txt and the body passage is in churn-body.txt. Adjudicate.
I'll compare the glossary's definition with the computation the body actually describes.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
METRICS GLOSSARY
Churn rate: the percentage of subscribers who cancel in a period, divided by the number of subscribers at the START of the period.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
REPORT BODY, SECTION 5 (excerpt)
"...churn for Q3 was 4.1%, computed as cancellations during the quarter divided by the average subscriber count across the quarter..."

The analyst is right: the body and the glossary describe two different denominators. The glossary defines churn as cancellations ÷ subscribers **at the start** of the period. Section 5 computed cancellations ÷ the **average** subscriber count across the quarter. In a growing subscriber base the average exceeds the start count, so the body's method systematically reports a lower churn rate than the glossary's method on identical cancellation data — the report is flattering itself by a definitional drift, not by any arithmetic error.

Neither method is 'wrong' in the abstract — average-base churn is a legitimate convention. What is wrong is the document set containing both while claiming one glossary. The number in section 5 cannot be compared with any quarter computed the glossary way, and a reader who checks the computation against the glossary will conclude the arithmetic is broken when actually the definition moved.

Resolution path: the metrics owner picks the house definition (my recommendation: keep the glossary's start-of-period base — it is the more common external convention, so benchmarks stay comparable), section 5's figure is recomputed on that base and republished with a note, and every other churn figure in the set is census-checked for which base it used. Then add the enforcement that prevents recurrence: figures in reports cite the glossary version they were computed under.

In July, 'Customer Services' was renamed 'Customer Experience'. Our document archive spans the rename. A researcher asks: should we update the old documents to the new name? The archive census is in archive.txt. Advise, with the reasoning.
Reading the census to see what the archive actually contains across the rename.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
ARCHIVE CENSUS
Documents dated Jan-Jun 2027 naming 'Customer Services': 214
Documents dated Jul-Dec 2027 naming 'Customer Experience': 167
Documents that are signed or filed (contracts, regulatory returns): 58 of the 381
Live templates still carrying the old name: 3

No — do not rewrite the archive, and the census shows why the question splits into three different answers for three different populations.

Of the 381 documents, 58 are signed or filed. Those are records of what was true when they were made: a contract signed with 'Customer Services' in March was signed with a department of that name, and editing it falsifies the record. They stay exactly as they are, forever.

The remaining historical documents (the unsigned reports, memos, guides) also stay — not for legal reasons but for findability and honesty: a reader researching the rename needs the old name present in old documents, and a silent global replace would make the July change invisible and break every quotation anyone has made from those documents.

What does change: the 3 live templates still carrying the old name — those are not history, they are the future being drafted wrong. And the archive gains one finding aid: a rename note in the index ('Customer Services became Customer Experience on 1 July 2027; search both names for full coverage'), plus dual-name tagging in the document register so searches under either name surface the whole run. The principle to record: archives are edited never, annotated readily, and templates are where a rename actually gets implemented.
Two documents in the same compliance pack use 'CA' and a reviewer got confused. The usages are in ca.txt. Untangle it.
Reading both usages in context to establish what CA means in each.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
DOCUMENT 1 (security standard)
"...certificates must be issued by an approved CA..."
"...the CA's root key is held offline..."
DOCUMENT 2 (site schedule)
"...the CA facility tour is scheduled for March..."
"...shipping address: Fresno, CA..."

The confusion is real and the pack created it: 'CA' carries three meanings across two documents. In the security standard, CA is the Certificate Authority — the organisation that issues certificates and holds a root key. In the site schedule, 'the CA facility' means the California facility, and 'Fresno, CA' is the postal abbreviation for California. Two of the three are the same two letters meaning a place; the third is an organisation — and the documents sit in one pack, cross-refer to each other, and are read by the same reviewers in one sitting.

The repair follows the standard collision rule: the abbreviation belongs to whichever meaning is *defined* in the pack (Certificate Authority, in the security standard's glossary), and the other uses get spelled out — 'the California facility', and postal addresses keep 'CA' only inside the address block where the convention is universal and unambiguous. What not to do: coin a replacement abbreviation for one side ('Calif.') — invented abbreviations just add a third thing to learn.

And log the collision in the style sheet. Abbreviation collisions are discovered one confused reviewer at a time; a collision register ('CA = Certificate Authority in this pack; do not use for California outside addresses') converts each discovery into permanent immunity for the document set.

Four authors each wrote a chapter of the annual review and I assembled them. The chapters' opening lines and their scene-setting lengths are in seams.txt. It reads strangely at the joins. Diagnose the seams.
Reading the chapter openings as a reader crossing the seams would.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
ASSEMBLED REPORT - OPENING LINES OF EACH CHAPTER
Ch 1: "This report reviews the division's year..." (412 words of scene-setting)
Ch 2: "This report reviews the division's year. Operations performance..." (368 words of scene-setting)
Ch 3: "This report reviews the division's year. The financial position..." (395 words of scene-setting)
Ch 4: "Customer outcomes are assessed against..." (no scene-setting)

The joins read strangely because three of the four authors each wrote the report's introduction. Chapters 1, 2 and 3 all open with 'This report reviews the division's year' and each then spends roughly 370–410 words setting the same scene — 1,175 words of scene-setting in total, most of it read three times by anyone who reads the report straight through. Each author, writing their chapter as a standalone file, quite reasonably introduced the whole report; the assembly inherited all three introductions.

Chapter 4 shows the counterfactual: its author assumed the earlier chapters existed and opened on its own subject — which is why its seam is the only smooth one.

Repair: keep Chapter 1's scene-setting (it is the report's real introduction), and cut Chapters 2 and 3 down to a one-paragraph chapter-level opening that starts from their own subjects, salvaging any sentence from their long openings that contains chapter-specific content the others lack. Brief the authors on the rule for next year — in an assembled document, only the first chapter introduces the whole; every other chapter introduces itself — and add it to the assembly checklist, because duplicated openings are the single most predictable seam defect in multi-author documents.

The strategy document's chapters were written by Finance and by Operations. A board member spotted that the two halves seem to assume different inflation rates. The relevant passages are in assum-a.txt and assum-b.txt. Verify and assess.
Comparing the two chapters' working assumptions directly.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 3 - FINANCIAL PLAN (excerpt)
"...costs are projected at the planning assumption of 2.0% annual inflation throughout the plan period..."

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 5 - OPERATIONS PLAN (excerpt)
"...with input costs rising at 3.5% a year, the operations budget builds in..."

The board member is right: the document plans on two different futures. Chapter 3 projects all costs at **2.0%** inflation 'throughout the plan period'; Chapter 5 builds its operations budget on **3.5%** input-cost inflation. The gap is 1.5 percentage points, compounding over the plan — on any cost line, the two chapters' year-3 figures for the same inputs diverge by roughly 4–5%.

Neither chapter is internally wrong; the document is. Each team used its own house assumption (Finance's planning rate, Operations' observed supplier rate), wrote it down honestly inside its own chapter, and the assembly process never compared assumptions across the seam — because assumptions live in prose, not in a table anyone reconciles.

Repairs: (1) immediate — the document gets one assumptions box, owned by Finance, stating the single planning rate, and Chapter 5's budget is either restated on it or explicitly presented as a sensitivity case ('operations costed at 3.5% as a stress case against the 2.0% plan'). Both readings are legitimate; the silent mixture is not. (2) structural — every assembled document carries an assumptions register as a front table, and the assembly checklist includes reading it against each chapter. Contradictions between chapters are almost never about facts; they are about assumptions nobody laid side by side.
Apply our style sheet to the submitted draft section. The sheet extract is in style.txt and the draft is in draft.txt. I want every fix cited to its rule — no silent edits.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
HOUSE STYLE SHEET (extract)
R1: Dates in body text as '14 March 2027'.
R2: Percentages with one decimal in tables, whole numbers in prose.
R3: Job titles lowercase except in headings.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
DRAFT SECTION (as submitted)
"On 03/14/2027, the Operations Manager confirmed that uptime reached 99.95 percent in tables and 99.95% in prose, and thanked the engineers, testers and support staff."

Four fixes, each cited:

1. **R1 (date format):** '03/14/2027' → '14 March 2027'. The draft's US slash format breaches R1 and is also the ambiguous pattern the sheet exists to kill.
2. **R2 (percentages):** '99.95 percent in tables' — the sentence describes a table value in prose form, but the value itself (99.95) carries two decimals where R2 allows one in tables: the table value should read 100.0% (rounded) or the underlying figure restated; and the prose mention '99.95%' breaches R2's whole-numbers-in-prose rule — it should read '100%' in prose or the sentence should be restructured so the precise figure lives only in the table. 3. **R3 (job titles):** 'the Operations Manager' → 'the operations manager' in body text.
4. **R4 (Oxford comma):** 'the engineers, testers and support staff' → 'the engineers, testers, and support staff'.

Fix 2 is the instructive one: a style pass is not authorised to change what a number says, only how it is presented — where presentation and substance collide (a rounding that turns 99.95 into 100), the style editor's job is to flag, not to fix. Knowing which of the two a given edit is, is the whole skill.

Two chapters of our company history were written by different people and the join is jarring. The closing of chapter 6 is in voice-a.txt and the opening of chapter 7 is in voice-b.txt. Locate the cliff and propose the bridge.
Reading the two passages back to back, as the reader meets them.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 6, CLOSING (excerpt)
"...and so, by the winter of 1987, the little firm that had begun in a rented garage employed two hundred people, and Margaret Ellison — who still answered the phone herself when it rang at lunchtime — had become, without ever quite deciding to, the head of a company."

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER 7, OPENING (excerpt)
"In FY1988 the organisation executed a headcount expansion of 214 FTEs and operationalised a second distribution facility, leveraging synergies across the logistics function."

The cliff is total: the two passages differ on every axis a voice has. Chapter 6 is narrative — past tense, named people, concrete detail (the phone at lunchtime), sentences that breathe. Chapter 7 opens in corporate-report register — fiscal-year dating, 'executed a headcount expansion', 'operationalised', 'leveraging synergies' — and, buried in the register change, it also contradicts the story: 200 people employed by winter 1987 becomes an 'expansion of 214 FTEs' in FY1988, numbers the reader cannot reconcile because the voices give them no bridge.

The repair is not to rewrite chapter 7 in chapter 6's voice wholesale — its author writes the operational chapters and some register difference is natural across a long book. The repair is a bridge: end chapter 6 (or open chapter 7) with a short transitional passage in the narrative voice that carries the reader across — two or three sentences that close the garage era ('The garage years ended the way they had begun, with Margaret...') and hand over ('What followed was growth of a different kind, counted in facilities and payrolls rather than in favours and phone calls'). Then let chapter 7's register soften by degrees over its first page rather than arriving at full corporate pitch in sentence one.

Also flag the numbers to the authors: 200 employed versus 214 FTE expansion needs one reconciling sentence regardless of voice, or the bridge will faithfully connect two chapters that disagree.

Our strategy document's introduction promises six pillars. I've a feeling the body only delivers five. The introduction is in intro.txt and the body's section list is in body-sections.txt. Check the promise against the delivery.
Comparing the introduction's promised structure with the sections the body actually contains.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
INTRODUCTION (excerpt)
"...this strategy rests on six pillars: Product, People, Partnerships, Process, Platform, and Presence in our communities..."

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
BODY SECTIONS
1. Product
2. People
3. Partnerships
4. Process
5. Platform

Your feeling is correct: the introduction promises six pillars and the body delivers five. **'Presence in our communities' has no section.** Product, People, Partnerships, Process and Platform each get their chapter; the sixth pillar is named in the introduction and never mentioned again.

This is the most dangerous species of missing section, because the document does not look incomplete — it looks finished. The table of contents matches the body; only the introduction remembers the promise. A reader who checks (a board member, a journalist, a community partner looking for their pillar) finds the gap instantly, and the charitable reading is carelessness while the uncharitable one is that the commitment was quietly dropped.

Two honest repairs, and the choice is the strategy owner's, not the editor's: (1) the pillar is real — commission the section, even a short one, before publication; the deadline moves or the section is brief, but the promise is kept. (2) The pillar was dropped in deliberation — then the introduction is corrected to five pillars and, because the six-pillar version has already circulated in draft, the change is acknowledged in the covering note. What must not happen is the third path: renumbering nothing, saying nothing, and hoping the introduction is read less carefully than the contents page. It never is, by the readers who matter.
I think the same safety paragraph appears in two chapters of the manual and the copies have drifted. Both instances are in dup-a.txt and dup-b.txt. Compare them word by word.

"Before any work on the pressure system, isolate the supply, vent the accumulator to below 2 bar, and confirm zero pressure on gauge P-114. Work must not begin until the duty holder has signed the permit."

The paragraphs are identical except for one number — and it is the number that matters most in the paragraph. Chapter 3 says vent the accumulator to below **2 bar**; Chapter 8 says below **5 bar**. I cannot tell you from the text which value is current — that belongs to the safety engineer, and this goes to them today as a blocking item, because technicians read whichever chapter their task points them to and the manual currently authorises two different thresholds for the same operation.

The structural repair, once the engineer rules: do not just fix the stale copy. Replace both instances with a single sourced procedure — the paragraph lives in one chapter, and the other chapter references it ('follow the isolation procedure in §3.4'). Duplicated safety text is a promise to diverge again; the next threshold change will again be made in one place. In manuals, duplication is not redundancy — it is a future inconsistency with a date on it.
A reviewer says the report 'explains things backwards'. The chapter map with each chapter's key dependencies is in chaptermap.txt. Test the claim.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
CHAPTER MAP
Ch 1 Overview - introduces: the programme
Ch 2 Costs - uses: the programme
Ch 3 Benefits - uses: the benefit model (introduced in Ch 6)
Ch 4 Risks - uses: costs
Ch 5 Recommendation - uses: the benefit model (Ch 6), the risk register (Ch 4)
Ch 6 The Benefit Model - introduces: the benefit model
Ch 7 Delivery - uses: the recommendation (Ch 5)

The reviewer is right, and the map shows the fault precisely: the benefit model is *introduced* in Chapter 6 but *used* in Chapters 3 and 5. A reader moving through the report meets the model's outputs (Chapter 3's benefits, Chapter 5's recommendation) three chapters before they meet the model itself — its assumptions, its inputs, its limits. Every judgement the reader forms about the benefits is formed before they are given the means to judge them.

Chapter 5's other dependency (the risk register from Chapter 4) is fine, and Chapter 7 using Chapter 5's recommendation is correct order. The single inversion is the benefit model's position.

Two repairs: (1) move the model chapter forward — renumber so the model precedes Benefits (order becomes Overview, Costs, Benefit Model, Benefits, Risks, Recommendation, Delivery). Clean, but it renumbers everything downstream and every cross-reference with it. (2) Leave the order and add a proper forward bridge: Chapter 3 opens with a half-page 'the model in brief' summary that states its assumptions and points to Chapter 6 for the full treatment. Weaker than (1) but sometimes right for a report whose chapters are read standalone by different audiences.

My recommendation is (1) for this report, because the recommendation chapter — the one the decision rests on — is a dependent of the model, and a decision document should never ask to be believed before it has shown its working. Whichever is chosen, add the dependency check to the assembly process: list each chapter's introduces/uses, and no chapter may use what a later chapter introduces without a deliberate bridge.

SECTION 9 - FINANCE CONTROLS (excerpt)
"...all supplier commitments above £25,000 require Finance Director approval. In the event of any inconsistency, this section prevails over other sections of this manual."

This is not a wording inconsistency; it is a genuine governance conflict with a self-referential twist. Section 4 routes supplier contracts above £50,000 to the Procurement Board and declares itself authoritative. messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
RETENTION FACTS
Contracts and signed agreements: legal requires execution versions + final drafts, kept 7 years after expiry.
Regulated reports (filed): the filed version is a legal record, kept permanently.
Internal procedures: no legal requirement; currently 14 versions of the expenses procedure retained.
Working drafts: no requirement; the store holds drafts of documents long since published.
Email attachments: uncontrolled duplicates of many of the above.

A defensible rule sorts versions by the *reason* they might be needed, and the facts give three distinct classes.

**Class 1 — keep exactly, by obligation.** Filed regulated reports: the filed version, permanently — it is the legal record of what was submitted, and no other version substitutes for it. Contracts: the execution version and the final draft, 7 years after expiry. Note the precision: the obligation attaches to specific versions (filed, executed, final), not to the whole version history — the 11 intermediate drafts of a filed report have no legal standing and keeping them adds discovery exposure without adding compliance.

**Class 2 — keep the current and one predecessor, by operational need.** Internal procedures (the expenses procedure's 14 versions): the current version is the working document; one predecessor is kept because 'what did the procedure say when this claim was made?' is a real question with a one-version reach. Versions older than the predecessor can go.

**Class 3 — delete on publication.** Working drafts of published documents: their entire value was becoming the published version. Retain the published version and the draft history collapses into it.

And the uncontrolled class — email attachments — is where the real volume and the real risk both sit: every 'kept' version above exists in uncontrolled duplicate in inboxes, outside any schedule. The retention rule must say so honestly: the schedule governs the store; attachments are addressed by mailbox retention policy, or the schedule is theatre. Put the rule, the classes, and the legal citations in one retention schedule document, owned and dated — a retention practice nobody wrote down is just deletion waiting to be second-guessed.

Volume labelled 'Harbour Survey 2026': its contents page lists chapters beginning 'Tidal flows', 'Berths', 'Dredging'. Its first bound chapter heading reads '1. Groundwater Levels'.
Volume labelled 'Groundwater Report 2026': its contents page lists 'Aquifers', 'Boreholes', 'Contamination'. Its first bound chapter heading reads '1. Tidal Flows'.

In the Harbour volume, the contents page lists harbour chapters (Tidal flows, Berths, Dredging) while the first bound chapter is 'Groundwater Levels'. Because the sample was drawn evenly across chapters (a stratified sample, not a convenience grab from the front), that projection is a defensible planning figure — with its uncertainty stated: on a sample of 60, the true rate could plausibly sit anywhere in a band of roughly 3% to 18%, so the honest sentence is 'we estimate around 40 broken references, plausibly between about 15 and 85'.

(2) Spend the remaining time not on more sampling but on the *classes* the sample exposed — if the 5 share a pattern (say, all cite a chapter that was renumbered), a targeted census of that class finds real breakages faster than random sampling finds statistical comfort. (3) Report it as what it was: a stratified sample of 60 of 480, 5 broken, estimate ~40 (band stated), with the sample's chapters listed. MANUAL EXCERPTS (retrieved for triage)
p.12: "...the product is warranted for two years from delivery..."
p.40 (extended-care chapter): "...during the three-year warranty period, extended-care customers receive..."

First the case, because triage starts with the text: both quotations are real, and they are *not* quite the contradiction the customer read. Page 12 states the standard warranty: two years from delivery. Page 40, inside the extended-care chapter, speaks of 'the three-year warranty period' for extended-care customers — the extended plan evidently stretches cover to three years, but page 40 never says that is what it means: it calls the extended arrangement simply 'the warranty period', colliding with page 12's term. Now the protocol this case illustrates, for every future report:

1. **Verify against the text** before replying — retrieve both passages; roughly a third of reported contradictions are misreadings, and the reply differs completely.
2. **Classify**: true contradiction (same population, two values), apparent contradiction (different populations, colliding wording — this case), or misreading. The class decides the fix: correct a value, clarify a term, or explain.
3. **Fix at the term level**: page 40 should read 'the extended-care cover period (three years)' and page 12 gains '(extended-care customers: see chapter 9)' — both pages change a little, so no future reader can collide them.
4. **Reply to the reporter with the finding and the fix**, thanking them specifically — a reader who reports an inconsistency is an unpaid auditor, and the reply they get decides whether the next one bothers.
5. **Log it** in the errata/fix register with the classification; a pattern of apparent contradictions around one term is a terminology problem asking for a census, not a series of one-off clarifications.

PROOF PASS FINDINGS
1. p.2: 'the supplier shall now provide monthly reports' — context shows 'shall not provide' was intended; the 't' of 'not' is missing (reads 'now').
2. p.3: 'unlimited liability' in a summary of a clause that caps liability (the clause says 'limited').
3. p.5: 'their' for 'there' (×3).
4. p.6: a figure typed as 12,500 in the summary; the source table says 125,000.
5. p.7: 'publically' misspelled.

Your suspicion is right: this list contains two meaning-inverting errors wearing the clothes of typos, and three genuine trivialities.

**Critical — fix before anything else moves:** Finding 1, 'shall now provide' for 'shall not provide'. A dropped letter converts a prohibition into an obligation — the single most dangerous typo class in legal text, and spellcheckers sail past it because 'now' is a word. Finding 2, 'unlimited' for 'limited' in the liability summary, inverts the clause it summarises; anyone who reads the summary instead of the clause (which is everyone, that is what summaries are for) carries away the opposite of the bargain. Finding 4, 12,500 for 125,000, is a dropped digit — a 10× error in a figure, in the same severity class even though it looks like a slip of the keyboard.

**Trivial:** 'their/there' (×3) and 'publically' — embarrassing, credibility-taxing, and incapable of changing an obligation, a figure, or a fact. Fix them in the same pass, but understand they are a different species.

The proofing lesson to institutionalise: a proof pass that treats all errors as equal will spend its attention on the visible ones. Run two passes with different eyes — a *meaning* pass hunting negations, qualifiers (limited/unlimited, may/must, before/after) and figures against their sources; and a *surface* pass for spelling and grammar. The meaning pass is the one that protects the company; the surface pass is the one that protects its dignity. Both matter; only one can bankrupt you.

Heading structure: 17 of 24 articles are sound; **7 skip levels or run multiple H1s**. Since headings are the table of contents a screen reader builds, a skipped level is a missing chapter in the only navigation those readers get — the same hierarchy fault as in print, with a less forgiving audience.

Link text: 31 of 212 links read 'click here' or 'here' (about 15%). Read aloud in a links list — which is how screen-reader users survey a page — they are 31 identical, meaningless entries. Tables: 9 of 12 have marked header rows; the 3 without are data tables a screen reader will read as undifferentiated streams.

Verdict: the set is inconsistent rather than uniformly poor — most articles pass most checks, which means the publishing process has no accessibility gate, only authors of varying habits. Remediation order follows user impact: alt attributes first (a census-driven fix, every image visited), heading structures second (restyle, as with print), link text third (31 rewrites, each saying where the link goes), table headers last. Then the systemic fix: the four checks above become an automated pre-publication scan — all four are mechanically detectable, and a defect a machine can catch should never again wait for an audit to find.

DOCUMENT CONTROL RECORDS - safety manual
Version history: v5.1 issued 2026-11-03 (approved: H. Whitfield, Safety Manager); v5.2 issued 2027-01-26 (approved: H. Whitfield); v6.0 issued 2027-03-15 (approved: S. Adeyemi, Head of Safety).
Change summary for v5.2: '§4.3 isolation sequence reordered; Annex B contact numbers updated; no other changes.'
Distribution: v5.2 issued to 14 registered holders; acknowledgements received from 14.

The evidence pack, assembled from the control records:

**Version in force on 14 February 2027: v5.2.** It was issued on 26 January 2027 and superseded by v6.0 on 15 March 2027, so it covers 14 February unambiguously — the version history alone answers the regulator's first question, which is exactly what a version history is for.

**Approved by:** H. Whitfield, Safety Manager — the same approver as v5.1, with the approval role changing hands only at v6.0 (S. Adeyemi, Head of Safety). The record shows named individuals with roles, not a department: accountability is attributable.

**Changes from the previous version (v5.1 → v5.2):** the recorded summary lists three items — §4.3's isolation sequence reordered, Annex B's contact numbers updated, and an explicit 'no other changes'. That closing phrase matters: it converts the summary from a sample into a claim of completeness, which is what makes it evidence rather than illustration.

**Distribution:** v5.2 went to 14 registered holders and all 14 acknowledged — so the pack can also show the in-force version actually reached its audience, the link most control systems fail to evidence.

One gap to note before this goes out, because the regulator will find it if I don't: the records show issue dates and approvers but not the *approval dates* themselves — if approval and issue were separated by weeks, the current records cannot show it. Recommend the control table gains an approval-date column from v6.1 onward; for this submission, the pack as assembled answers the three questions asked, completely, from records kept at the time — which is the definition of document control done right.

AUDIT PACK - draft divisional annual report
REFERENCES: 3 in-text section references checked against headings: §2 cites '§5' for risk; risk is §6. §4 cites '§3.2' (exists). Introduction cites '§7' for outlook; outlook is §7.
FIGURES: headline profit £2.31m (summary) vs £2.13m (body §3) vs appendix rows 918 + 764 + 447 (thousands) with printed total 2,129 (thousands).
TERMS: the division's product called 'the Platform' 41 times and 'the Portal' 17 times.
DATES: report covers 'the year to 31 March 2027'; §6 states the risk review was 'conducted in April 2027' and is presented as covering the year.
STRUCTURE: contents lists 7 sections; body has 7 sections; §5 is titled 'People' in contents and 'People and Culture' in body.

**CONSISTENCY AUDIT — draft divisional annual report. Verdict: NOT READY. Five findings, two blocking.**

**F1 (figures, BLOCKING).** The headline profit exists in three versions: summary £2.31m, body £2.13m, and the appendix — whose rows foot to 2,129 thousand = £2.129m, matching its printed total of 2,129. The appendix and the body agree (£2.13m); the summary's £2.31m is a digit transposition of 2.13 and overstates profit by £180,000 in the one figure every reader will quote. Repair: summary conforms to £2.13m; the appendix is authoritative because it shows its working.

**F2 (references, BLOCKING).** §2 cites '§5' for risk; risk is §6 (a chapter was inserted ahead of it). The other two sampled references (§3.2, §7) are correct. Repair: repoint to §6, then run the full reference census — one stale reference from a known insertion means every reference downstream of that insertion is suspect, not just this one.

**F3 (terms, medium).** The product is 'the Platform' 41 times and 'the Portal' 17 times. One product, two names, no stated distinction. Repair: the product's owner names it once, the census list drives the conforming edits, and the rejected name goes on the do-not-use list.

**F4 (dates, medium).** §6 presents an April 2027 risk review as covering a year that ended 31 March 2027. Either the review's coverage is misstated or the report's period is — the owner must declare which; a review conducted after the period can *report on* the year but the sentence must say so.

**F5 (structure, low).** §5 is 'People' in the contents and 'People and Culture' in the body — regenerate the contents from the headings at production.

Repair plan, in order: F1 and F2 today (both are single-point fixes with census follow-ups), F3 with the product owner this week, F4 as a declared-basis correction, F5 at production. Re-verification: I re-run the figure triangle and the full reference census on the corrected draft; the audit closes on evidence, not on assurances. That is the whole method, and it scales from this report to any document too long to hold in one head: census what can be counted, trace what must agree, and never let a summary carry a number its own appendix cannot prove.

messages.content:
INCIDENT FACTS
The catalogue's price table listed the Model R pump at £1,850; the correct price was £2,150.
The price came from a spreadsheet export dated January; prices were revised in February; the catalogue was assembled in March from the January export.
The catalogue passed a proofread (spelling, layout) and a price spot-check of 5 items — the Model R was not among them.
No document in the chain recorded which price-list version it used.

**Root cause.** The error was not a typo and not carelessness at the point of printing: the catalogue was assembled from a *stale source*. The price table was drawn from the January spreadsheet export; prices were revised in February; the March assembly never re-pulled them, and nothing in the chain recorded which price-list version the catalogue used, so the staleness was invisible to everyone downstream. Each individual step was performed competently — the proofread proofread, the spot-check checked — and the system still shipped a wrong price, because no step in the process owned the question 'is this source current?'

Contributing factors, honestly stated: the spot-check of 5 prices could not have caught a systematic staleness (checking a stale table's entries against themselves proves nothing — the check compared the catalogue to the same export it was built from); and the February price revision was never announced to document owners, so the catalogue team had no signal to re-pull.

**The change that prevents recurrence** — three parts, all cheap: (1) **Source citation**: every document that carries prices (or any volatile figure) states its source and version on the document itself ('Prices from price list v2027.02'), so staleness is visible at a glance. (2) **Currency gate**: the pre-publication checklist gains one line — 'source versions confirmed current at assembly date' — signed by the assembler; a catalogue assembled in March from a January export fails the gate on its face. (3) **Change notification**: the price list's owner notifies registered document owners on every revision, and the register of documents carrying prices is maintained — the same key-figures register discipline as for corrected figures.

What the review should *not* recommend: 'more careful proofreading'. The proofreaders were careful; the process sent them a document whose defect was in its provenance, not its text. Fix the provenance, and the next February revision — there will be one — arrives as a routine re-pull instead of a week of honouring £1,850.
